newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr's dive threatens Japan foreign bond investment.
newsitem.headline: Dlr's dive threatens Japan foreign bond investment.

text.p: The dollar's dive is likely to put a dampener on Japan's foreign bond buying spree, making individual investors wary of dollar-based assets, underwriters and traders said on Monday.
Rock-bottom Japanese interest rates have sent yield-hungry Japanese individual investors flocking to foreign bonds in recent months, particularly dual-currency issues.

But the dollar's steep and rapid slide has slashed the yen value of those investments and made issuers reluctant to launch fresh bonds, as individual investors are bound to think twice about putting more of their money in foreign bonds.
The dollar has taken a dive of nearly 10 yen since early May, trading as low as 117.50 yen in Tokyo on Monday before recovering to around 119 yen.
"Until the trend of the dollar becomes clear, we cannot offer new foreign bonds to individual investors for a while," said a manager at the investment division of a major Japanese brokerage.
"Lots of uncertainties surround the U.S. currency at the moment," he added.
Many Japanese brokerages had been planning to offer massive amounts of foreign bonds to absorb a substantial pool of money from small investors in the run-up to Japan's summer bonus season in June.

Japanese private investors have poured some 10 trillion yen ($84.7 billion) worth of funds overseas in the last few years in the form of foreign bond investment, including popular dual currency samurais and Eurobonds. The dollar's steady comeback from historic lows plumbed in 1995 had emboldened individual investors to put money into foreign bonds.
But they are likely to turn cautious now after being burnt by the dollar's sudden reversal of course, underwriters said.
Traders said investors were already suffering heavy losses on risky foreign exchange option-linked dual currency bonds offered in recent months.
Such option-linked bonds enable bond holders to receive high coupons in yen at maturity only if foreign exchange rates stay above levels agreed at the time of the launch.

The coupon of such dual-currency bonds, usually set at 4.0-4.5 percent, is paid in yen, while the bonds, usually with maturities of three to six months, are redeemed in foreign currencies, mostly U.S. dollars.
In other words, the bonds are profitable as long as foreign exchange rates do not fall below a certain level, but investors have to take heavy losses if they break below that level.
The so-called "knockout" level for most of those options is estimated to have been set at 118 to 120 yen, with some at 115-117 yen, traders said.
At those levels, the terms of the bonds change to the severe financial disadvantage of the holder.

"It's like many land mines are hidden at various levels below 120 yen. Many have already exploded after the (dollar's) plunge," said a senior underwriter at a Japanese securities firm. "It's still possible that more could be hidden."
One underwriter said about 170 billion yen ($1.44 billion) worth of option-linked bonds had been offered in April, but the amount could be even larger if it included privately placed ones.
In the face of the dollar's nosedive, other dual-currency bonds which are due to be launched this month are likely to be left unsold, underwriters said.
A total of six dual-currency samurai bonds worth 150 billion yen ($1.27 billion) are scheduled to be issued from Monday through to the end of May.

"Private investors could steer clear of investing in dual-currency bonds with a fixed currency rate attached, after seeing the dollar's sharp dive," said Hisao Hosoya, manager of the corporate research section at Kokusai Securities.
"Private investors have enjoyed forex gains (until recently). But if the dollar fails to resume its upward trend, they may become more wary of fresh purchases," Hosoya said.
Hosoya said, however, that if dollar stabilises, Japanese investors may again look further afield for higher returns. ($1=118 yen)
